module_title: Installation Techniques for Non-Metal Roofing Sheets

lessons.title: Fiber Cement Sheet Installation
lessons.body:
Fiber cement sheets are heavy, brittle, and long-lasting. In Africa, they are common in high-rainfall areas because they resist rot and insects. To install, you need at least two people. Start by checking your roof structure: purlins should be at 600 mm to 750 mm centres for 6 mm sheets, and 900 mm for 8 mm sheets. Use timber or steel purlins treated against termites. Always wear gloves, dust mask, and eye protection when cuttingâfiber cement dust is harmful.

Lay sheets from the bottom edge (eaves) upward, working across the roof. Overlap side laps by one corrugation and end laps by 150 mm. Pre-drill holes 2 mm larger than the nail shank to allow for expansion. Use galvanised or stainless steel screws with rubber washers, driven into the crest of the corrugation, not the valley. Drive screws just until the washer compressesâover-tightening cracks the sheet. For a 3 m sheet, use at least 5 fasteners per purlin. On steep roofs, use safety harnesses and roof ladders.

Cut fiber cement with a diamond blade or fiber cement shear. Avoid abrasive discs that create dust. For ridges, use matching fiber cement ridge caps, fixed with screws and sealed with neutral-cure silicone. At eaves, install a 50 mm overhang and a drip edge to direct water into the gutter. In coastal areas, use stainless steel fasteners to avoid corrosion. After installation, wash the roof to remove dust and check for leaks with a water hose. Maintenance: inspect annually for cracked sheets and loose fasteners. Replace cracked sheets immediately to prevent water damage.

lessons.title: Asphalt Sheet Shingle Installation
lessons.body:
Asphalt shingles are popular for pitched roofs in Africa because they are lightweight, easy to cut, and relatively cheap. They come in strips or individual tabs. You need a clean, dry, smooth deckâusually plywood or OSB at least 12 mm thick, nailed at 150 mm centres. Cover the deck with a waterproof underlayment (felt or synthetic) overlapping 100 mm horizontally and 150 mm vertically. In hot climates, choose light-coloured shingles to reflect heat.

Start at the eaves with a starter stripâcut the tabs off a shingle and nail it along the edge, overlapping the drip edge by 10 mm. Nail with 25 mm galvanised roofing nails, 6 per shingle, placed 25 mm above the tab cuts and 12 mm from edges. Drive nails straight and flushânot into the shingle. Work upward in rows, offsetting each row by half a tab so joints don't align. In high-wind areas, use six nails per shingle and apply a dab of asphalt cement under each tab. For valleys, use a 900 mm wide metal valley flashing or woven method. On ridges, use pre-formed ridge caps or cut shingles and bend them over, nailing both sides.

In hot African climates, shingles can soften; avoid walking on them during the hottest part of the day. Clean cut edges with a sharp utility knife on a scrap board. Keep shingles in the shade before installationâthey tear easily when hot. After installation, press down all tabs and check for exposed nails. Seal any nail heads with asphalt cement. Inspect after storms for lifted tabs and re-seal. Expect 15â20 years life with proper ventilation.

lessons.title: Plastic and Composite Sheet Installation
lessons.body:
Plastic and composite sheetsâsuch as polycarbonate, PVC, and fibreglass-reinforced polyesterâare lightweight, translucent, and rust-proof. They are ideal for verandas, carports, and skylights. Most come in corrugated or trapezoidal profiles. They expand and contract with heat, so you must allow for movement. Use purlins at 600â900 mm centres, depending on sheet thickness. Never use them near open flamesâthey melt and drip.

Install from the leeward side (away from prevailing wind) to avoid wind-driven rain. Overlap side laps by one corrugation and end laps by 100â150 mm. Pre-drill holes 3â4 mm larger than the screw diameter. Use screws with neoprene or EPDM washers and plastic caps. Drive screws into the crest, not the valley. Do not over-tightenâthe sheet must be able to move. For long sheets, use a expansion gap of 5 mm per 3 m length at the end. Cut with a fine-tooth saw, jigsaw, or angle grinder with a metal cutting discâbut keep speed low to avoid melting. Wear goggles and gloves.

For ridges, use matching plastic ridge caps fixed with screws and sealed with silicone. At eaves, allow a 50â75 mm overhang and install a foam closure strip to keep out insects and dust. In dusty areas, clean sheets with mild soap and waterânever solvents. For composite sheets with a gel coating, avoid walking on them when hot. Fasten with screws that have a low-profile head. Check for cracks around fasteners after a few months. Replace any sheet that shows crazing or yellowing. These sheets last 10â15 years in African sun if UV-stabilised.

lessons.title: Adhesives and Fasteners for Non-Metal Sheets
lessons.body:
Choosing the right fasteners and adhesives is critical for non-metal roofing sheets. For fiber cement, use galvanised or stainless steel screws with rubber washersânever plain steel, which rusts and stains. Screw length should penetrate the purlin by at least 25 mm. For asphalt shingles, use 25â30 mm galvanised roofing nails with 10 mm heads. In coastal areas, use stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised. For plastic sheets, use screws with neoprene washers and plastic caps; metal washers can crack the sheet. Always pre-drill to avoid cracking.

Adhesives are used for sealing laps, ridges, and flashings. For fiber cement, use neutral-cure silicone or polyurethane sealant. For asphalt shingles, use asphalt roofing cement (black mastic) or modified bitumen tape. For plastic and composite, use silicone or MS polymer adhesiveânot solvent-based adhesives that attack plastic. Apply adhesive in a continuous bead, not dots. Clean surfaces with a dry cloth before applying. In hot climates, choose high-temperature adhesives that won't soften.

Fastener spacing: for fiber cement, 5 screws per sheet per purlin; for asphalt, 6 nails per shingle; for plastic, 4â6 screws per square metre. Always drive fasteners perpendicular to the sheet. Use a screw gun with adjustable torque to avoid over-driving. For ridges and edges, use longer screws. Keep a supply of spare washers and caps. Inspect fasteners annuallyâtighten loose ones and replace rusted ones. In termite-prone areas, use steel or treated timber purlins. Never mix metalsâgalvanic corrosion will destroy the roof. Store fasteners in a dry place to prevent rust.

lessons.title: Edge Details and Ridge Caps
lessons.body:
Edge details and ridge caps protect the most vulnerable parts of the roof: the eaves, gables, and ridges. At the eaves, install a drip edge (metal flashing) under the underlayment and over the fascia board. It should extend 50 mm over the gutter. For fiber cement, use a fiber cement barge board or metal flashing. For asphalt shingles, the drip edge goes under the starter strip. For plastic sheets, use a foam closure strip between the sheet and the purlin to block wind and insects. Secure with screws every 300 mm.

Ridge caps cover the peak where two roof planes meet. For fiber cement, use matching fiber cement ridge pieces, bedded in silicone and screwed at 300 mm centres. For asphalt shingles, cut shingles into three tabs and bend them over the ridge, overlapping each by 50 mm, nailing both sides. For plastic, use pre-formed ridge caps with matching profile, fixed with screws and sealed with silicone. In all cases, the ridge cap must overlap the sheets by at least 100 mm on each side. For hips (where ridges meet at an angle), use hip caps or cut shingles to fit.

Gable edges (rake) need a barge board or metal flashing to prevent wind uplift. Fix with screws at 200 mm centres. For all edge details, use corrosion-resistant materials: aluminium, galvanised steel, or stainless steel. In coastal areas, avoid galvanisedâuse aluminium or stainless. Seal all joints with neutral-cure silicone. Check edges after storms; re-seal if lifted. Proper edge details stop water from creeping under sheets and extend roof life by years.

lessons.title: Ventilation and Moisture Control
lessons.body:
Without ventilation, non-metal roofs trap heat and moisture, causing condensation, mould, and premature failure. In Africa, the sun heats the roof, and at night the temperature drops, causing condensation on the underside. To prevent this, you need continuous airflow from eaves to ridge. Install soffit vents at the eaves (at least 1/150 of the roof area) and ridge vents at the peak. For every 1 mÂ² of roof, provide 1000 mmÂ² of vent area. Use insect mesh to keep out bugs. In hot climates, a reflective foil under the sheets can reduce heat gain.

For fiber cement and plastic sheets, leave a 25â50 mm gap between the sheet and any insulation. For asphalt shingles, ensure the attic space is ventilatedâuse gable vents or turbine vents. In humid coastal areas, use a dehumidifier or ensure cross-ventilation. If you have a cathedral ceiling (no attic), use a ventilated ridge and soffit vents. Never block vents with insulation. For flat roofs (less than 10Â° slope), use a vapour barrier under the sheets and a ventilated air gap above the deck.

Moisture control also means proper flashing around chimneys, pipes, and walls. Use lead or aluminium flashing, sealed with silicone. Ensure gutters are clean and drain away from the building. In thatched or shingle roofs, use a breathable underlayment. Check for leaks after heavy rain. If you see mould, improve ventilation and clean with a mild bleach solution. For plastic sheets, condensation can dripâinstall a anti-condensation felt or fleece on the underside. Regular inspection: check vents, flashings, and gutters twice a year. Good ventilation extends roof life and keeps the building comfortable.

quiz.q: What is the recommended purlin spacing for 6 mm fiber cement sheets?
quiz.explanation: 6 mm fiber cement sheets require purlins at 600-750 mm centres to prevent sagging and cracking.

quiz.q: How should you cut fiber cement sheets?
options: A) With a diamond blade or fiber cement shear
quiz.explanation: Diamond blades or fiber cement shears reduce dust and give clean cuts without cracking.

quiz.q: When installing fiber cement sheets, where do you drive screws?
options: A) In the valley of the corrugation
B) In the crest of the corrugation
quiz.explanation: Driving screws in the crest prevents water from pooling around the fastener and ensures a tight seal.

quiz.q: What is the minimum end lap for fiber cement sheets?
quiz.explanation: A 150 mm end lap provides adequate weatherproofing against wind-driven rain.

quiz.q: Why should you pre-drill holes for fiber cement sheets?
options: A) To make screws easier to drive
B) To allow for thermal expansion
quiz.explanation: Pre-drilling 2 mm larger than the screw shank allows the sheet to expand and contract without cracking.

quiz.q: What type of fasteners should be used for fiber cement in coastal areas?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel resists corrosion from salt air, unlike galvanised or plain steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended deck material for asphalt shingles?
options: A) Plywood or OSB at least 12 mm thick
quiz.explanation: A solid, smooth deck of plywood or OSB provides a stable base for shingles.

quiz.q: How many nails are typically used per asphalt shingle in high-wind areas?
quiz.explanation: Six nails per shingle increase wind resistance, especially in exposed areas.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a starter strip in asphalt shingle installation?
options: A) To provide a decorative edge
B) To seal the eaves and prevent wind uplift
quiz.explanation: The starter strip fills the gap at the eaves and helps prevent wind-driven rain from entering.

quiz.q: How should you offset asphalt shingle rows?
options: B) Offset by half a tab
C) Offset by one full tab
quiz.explanation: Offsetting by half a tab prevents water from seeping through aligned joints.

quiz.q: In hot climates, why should you avoid walking on asphalt shingles during the hottest part of the day?
options: B) They soften and can be damaged
C) They become too hot to touch
quiz.explanation: Heat softens asphalt shingles, making them prone to scuffing and tearing under foot traffic.

quiz.q: What type of underlayment is recommended for asphalt shingles?
quiz.explanation: Felt or synthetic underlayment provides a secondary water barrier and protects the deck.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of plastic and composite roofing sheets?
options: B) They are rust-proof and lightweight
quiz.explanation: Plastic and composite sheets resist rust and are easy to handle due to their low weight.

quiz.q: How much larger should pre-drilled holes be for plastic sheets compared to screw diameter?
quiz.explanation: A 3-4 mm clearance allows for thermal expansion without cracking the sheet.

quiz.q: Where should screws be driven on corrugated plastic sheets?
quiz.explanation: Driving in the crest ensures the washer seals properly and prevents water pooling.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean plastic roofing sheets?
quiz.explanation: Mild soap and water clean without damaging the plastic; solvents can cause crazing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended end lap for plastic sheets?
quiz.explanation: A 100-150 mm end lap provides a watertight seal while allowing for expansion.

quiz.q: Why should you install plastic sheets from the leeward side?
options: B) To prevent wind-driven rain from entering laps
quiz.explanation: Starting from the leeward side ensures laps face away from prevailing wind, reducing rain penetration.

quiz.q: What type of adhesive is suitable for sealing plastic sheets?
quiz.explanation: Silicone or MS polymer adhesives are compatible with plastics and remain flexible.

quiz.q: For fiber cement, what is the minimum screw penetration into the purlin?
quiz.explanation: At least 25 mm penetration ensures the screw holds securely in the purlin.

quiz.q: Which fastener is best for asphalt shingles in coastal areas?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel resists salt corrosion better than galvanised or plain steel.

quiz.q: How should adhesive be applied for roofing laps?
quiz.explanation: A continuous bead ensures a complete seal against water penetration.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a foam closure strip at the eaves?
options: B) To block wind, rain, and insects
quiz.explanation: Closure strips fill the gap between the sheet profile and purlin, preventing drafts and pest entry.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap for ridge caps on fiber cement?
quiz.explanation: A 100 mm overlap on each side ensures the ridge cap covers the sheet ends properly.

quiz.q: How are asphalt shingle ridge caps typically made?
options: B) By cutting shingles into tabs and bending them
D) By using fiber cement pieces
quiz.explanation: Cutting shingles into individual tabs and bending them over the ridge is a common method.

quiz.q: What material should be used for edge flashing in coastal areas?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium or stainless steel resist salt corrosion better than galvanised steel.

quiz.q: What is the minimum vent area required per 1 mÂ² of roof?
quiz.explanation: 1000 mmÂ² of vent area per square metre of roof ensures adequate airflow.

quiz.q: Where should soffit vents be installed?
options: C) In the middle of the roof
quiz.explanation: Soffit vents at the eaves allow cool air to enter and rise toward the ridge.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor ventilation in a roof?
quiz.explanation: Condensation and mould indicate trapped moisture due to inadequate ventilation.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect roof vents, flashings, and gutters?
quiz.explanation: Twice-yearly inspections catch problems early, especially before rainy seasons.
